Creator Breakdown · @nategaffney

How Nate Gaffney Went From 10K to 910K Followers in 91 Days by Letting People Be Self-Centered

By Martin Wang · Creative Mode · 100 Reels, Jul 2 to Oct 18, 2026

In July, Nate Gaffney posted 46 Reels. All 46 together earned 1.48 million views. Then on July 30 he posted one 31-second video that earned 3.57 million on its own.

He didn't buy a new camera, move to a new spot or change his hat. He changed who the video was about. Most creators make videos about themselves or their topic. Nate makes videos about you, and then hands you a reason to send it to someone.

I know it works because I tested it. I adapted parts of Nate's strategy to my own niche, and my account went from 50K to 249K followers in 55 posts.

→

Here's what Nate did, and how you can do it too.

Followers, in his own words

To find out exactly what changed, I went through his last 100 Reels. I watched every video frame by frame, read all 100 transcripts, and logged the views, likes and comments on each one. That's 57,772,119 views of data, scored against his median of 141,925 views per Reel.

I spent the last 48 hours analyzing and putting together this report so you can take away the strategy for yourself in just 10 minutes of reading.

Who this strategy is for

  • Anyone building a personal brand who is willing to talk to a camera for 60 to 90 seconds.
  • Creators in almost any niche: fitness, money, parenting, careers, relationships, faith, food, hobbies, creative work. If your audience is made of people, it fits.
  • Coaches, consultants and experts who want reach beyond the people who already know their topic.
  • Creators stuck posting tips or motivation with flat views. That's exactly where Nate was in July.

Who this is not for

  • Company brands like Coca-Cola or a software company, where the account speaks for a product and not a person.
  • Shops and product pages whose content has to show the product to sell it.
  • News and commentary accounts whose posts depend on what happened today.
  • Anyone who won't show their face or voice. The format runs on one person talking to you.
The surprising stat

95% of his views came from videos about other people

I sorted all 100 Reels into three content pillars. Videos describing a type of person took almost every view. His creator tips and his pep talks, 52 Reels between them, barely registered.

Not one of the 52 non-people Reels reached 5x his median. Of the 48 people Reels, 24 did.

His 28 series episodes took 70.9% of all views with a median of 7.0x. His 62 regular talking-head Reels had a median of 0.22x. Same face, same captions, same backyard.

The turn

One video split his account in two

Before July 30, his median Reel scored 0.09x. After it, 3.67x. Since August 21 he has posted 21 people Reels, and every single one beat 2.2x.

Every Reel in posting order, scored against his median (log scale)
25.2x · 3.57M views · Jul 30"Somebody said today that intellectual omnivores are the most interesting people."

Before this, his feed was pep talks ("Hey, ask for more. Go bigger.") and how-to videos for small creators. Then he described a type of person, said why they're great, and closed with: "If you've got some in your life, send this video to them and just say hey dude you're great."

The video was about the viewer and the friend they were picturing. Nobody watching it had to care about Nate.

The hook

"There's a rare breed of person who is both…"

Once he found the topic, he found the sentence. 21 Reels open with some version of it. They're 21% of his posts and 60% of his views, and 8 of his top 10.

Hook patterns: share of all views (number of Reels, median score)
"There's a rare breed of person out there who is both empathetic and a strong pattern recognizer. And these people are usually always right when somebody is shady."6.08M views · 42.8x · Aug 24
42.8x · 6.08M viewsThere's a rare breed of person out there who is both empathetic and a strong pattern recognizer.30.4x · 4.31M viewsThere's a rare breed of person who is very highly empathetic, but who is an absolute menace.27.6x · 3.92M viewsThere is a very rare type of person who has extremely strong pattern recognition but is playful about it.15.3x · 2.17M viewsThere's a rare breed of human out there who is both sassy and empathetic.

All 21 hit at least 2x. 15 of them hit 5x or more. No other opener he tried comes close to that hit rate.

Subtle pattern 1

A virtue plus a little mischief beats two virtues

Inside the "rare breed" formula there are two kinds of pairs. Some stack two virtues (kind and ambitious). Others pair a virtue with something cheeky (empathetic but a menace). The cheeky pairs win by double.

Every "rare breed" Reel, by type of pair. Tap a bar to watch it.

The 13 virtue-plus-mischief Reels have a median of 11.1x and 7 of them crossed 10x. The 8 virtue-plus-virtue Reels have a median of 5.4x and 2 crossed 10x. The virtue makes the viewer feel seen. The mischief makes it funny and specific enough that they picture one exact friend.

Subtle pattern 2

The funny job-title comparison

In October he added one more line to the hook: a serious job paired with a ridiculous one. He used it 4 times, and all 4 cleared 7x with a median of 12.4x.

Subtle pattern 3

Same trait, different partner, 32x the views

Watch what happens to one trait, pattern recognition, as he pairs it with different second traits. On its own it was a 1.3x video. Paired with empathy, it became his biggest Reel ever.

"Pattern recognition" Reels, by the trait it was paired with
1.33x · 189K viewsPattern recognition, alone42.8x · 6.08M viewsPattern recognition + empathy27.6x · 3.92M viewsPattern recognition + playfulness13.8x · 1.95M viewsPattern recognition + sarcasm

The lesson: when a trait works, keep it and swap the partner. The audience for "pattern recognizers" was already proven. Each new pairing found a new friend to send it to.

Subtle pattern 4

He re-shoots his winners

Three of his early people Reels were remade a few days later as numbered series episodes. Two of the three remakes beat a strong original.

TopicOriginalRemake
Intellectual omnivores25.2x · Jul 3017.2x · Aug 3, "Episode 1"
Dialectical thinkers5.6x · Aug 210.2x · Aug 7
Awkward people3.9x · Aug 310.2x · Aug 7

A topic that worked once is proof the audience exists. A remake 4 to 5 days later reaches the people who missed it, and it costs nothing to think up.

Subtle pattern 5

He knew the theory weeks before it worked

In July he posted the exact principle behind his later growth, twice. Both videos flopped. Knowing the idea wasn't enough. He had to turn it into a person the viewer could point at.

0.08x · 11K viewsJul 9: "Make your audience feel seen… I just started holding up a mirror."0.07x · 10K viewsJul 19: "Shareable content needs to satisfy both the person watching and the person they send it to."0.05x · 6K viewsJul 9: "Someone was telling me about the subjectivity barrier theory." Same hook, no person to send it to.

Even the "someone said" hook failed when the subject was a theory about everyone. It only worked once the subject was a type of person you could send it to.

Engine

Awareness and funnel

Strangers at the top, creators at the bottom

Nate's views and Nate's buyers are different people. His people Reels reach anyone curious about humans. His milestone Reels then turn the creators inside that crowd into leads for his series playbook and his series-writing service.

Top of funnel96.6%of views
Problem unaware · 70 Reels

People Reels and pep talks. No problem to solve, just "this is you" or "this is your friend". The biggest possible audience, and only the people Reels worked: 95.4% of views versus 1.1% for pep talks.

Middle1.4%of views
Problem and solution aware · 22 Reels

Creator how-tos like "How I make 10 to 20 Reels a day" and "Talking to the camera 101". Only small creators care, so reach stays low. He stopped posting these in August.

Bottom25%of comments
Product aware and most aware · 8 Reels

"10K to 300K in 28 days. Comment SERIES for the playbook." The series itself is the proof, so every viral episode doubles as a case study. Comment rate is 2.6%, 16x his people Reels. His bio closes the loop: "Let's write your content series."

The takeaway for you: let your widest content earn attention, then post the occasional results Reel that names your offer. Nate didn't need his top-of-funnel videos to be about his product.

Story or teaching?

Neither. He holds up a mirror

I tagged each Reel by what it does for the viewer. "Mirror" Reels describe the viewer or someone they know. They took 93% of his views.

What's on screen

The look never changes

Every episode uses the same kit: handheld medium shot outside against house siding, a white rounded title card naming the type, word-by-word serif captions, and an "Interesting People, For Curious Humans" card about 8 seconds in. A viewer can recognize the series with the sound off.

Interesting People · For Curious HumansThe series card, about 8 seconds in13.9x · 1.97M viewsThere's a rare breed of person who is sneaky smart.13.0x · 1.85M viewsThere's this rare type of person who is extremely intelligent, but also deeply mischievous.11.1x · 1.57M viewsThere is a rare kind of person who has the emotional intelligence of a seasoned therapist, but with the mouth of a sailo…16.9x · 2.40M viewsThere is a type of person who is both empathetic and analytical.
TLDR · The compact value

The core pattern

Describe a rare person the viewer either is or knows, then give them a reason to send it.

That's the whole machine. Three parts make it work, listed here from least to most important.

3
Least important

The series wrapper

Right after the hook he says the same line every time:

"Welcome to Interesting People for Curious Humans. If you like thinking about thinking, or talking about why people are the way that they are, this series is for you."

Why it works: It tells a new viewer what they get if they follow, and the name plus the title card make every episode recognizable. People Reels with this intro have a median of 7.9x, against 2.7x without it.

How to use it: "Welcome to [series name]. If you [what your viewer loves], this series is for you." Keep it under 8 seconds. A money creator could say: "Welcome to Money Personalities. If you've ever wondered why your friends spend the way they do, this series is for you." See Analytical Empath (16.9x).

2
Important

The two-exit close

39 of his 48 people Reels end almost word for word like this:

"If you know somebody like this, send this video to them. Let them know [a compliment]. And if this is you, welcome. I think you just found your people."

Why it works: It gives the viewer two jobs. Either they send it, which is the strongest signal Instagram tracks, or they recognize themselves and follow. The compliment turns a share into a gift, so it doesn't feel like spam.

How to use it: Tailor the compliment to the type. For the menace: "Maybe throw in a roast." For the sneaky smart one: "Let them know you're onto them." A parenting creator might close with: "If you know a slow rescue parent, send this to them and tell them their kids are going to be fine." See Emotionally Intelligent Menace (30.4x).

1
Most important

The contrast pair

"There's a rare breed of person who is both [virtue] and [lovable flaw]. They have the [skill] of a [serious job], but the [trait] of a [silly animal or job]."

Why it works: The word "rare" flatters. The virtue lets the viewer feel seen, which is the self-centered part. The flaw makes it specific and funny, so the viewer instantly thinks of one person to send it to. Virtue-plus-flaw pairs scored a 11.1x median.

How to use it: Keep a trait you know works and swap the partner, the way pattern recognition went from 1.3x alone to 42.8x with empathy. In personal finance: "There's a rare breed of person who saves aggressively but feels guilty spending a cent on themselves. The discipline of a monk, the spending confidence of a kid caught with a cookie." See Pattern Recognition & Playfulness (27.7x).

The takeaway

How to apply it to your niche

  1. Pick the people your audience cares about. That might be the audience itself (nurses, founders, new moms, gamers) or the people in their lives.
  2. Write two lists. List 10 virtues people in that world are proud of and 10 lovable flaws they joke about. Every virtue-flaw combo is a video idea, so 10 by 10 gives you 100. For money: "saves aggressively" plus "feels guilty spending" gives you the guilty saver.
  3. Name the type and write the hook. Give each combo a name people can repeat, like "the slow rescue parent". Then: "There's a rare breed of [person] who is both [virtue] and [flaw]." Add one serious-job vs silly-job comparison.
  4. Explain why the combo is rare in 60 to 90 seconds. Say "they", not "you", so the viewer can picture a specific friend. His winners ran 65 to 100 seconds.
  5. Close with both exits. Send it to them with a compliment, and "if this is you, welcome."
  6. Wrap it in a named series with a title card and a recurring intro line. Re-shoot any topic that hits 5x within a week.
  7. Cash in on the spikes. After a big week, post a milestone Reel with a comment keyword for a free resource. Your people Reels bring the reach, and the milestone Reel turns it into leads.
Real examples

What this looks like in other niches

Each one names a type of person, pairs a virtue with a lovable flaw, and has someone obvious to send it to.

Personal finance

The guilty saver

Saves aggressively, but feels guilty spending money on themselves.

"There's a rare breed of person who can save 40% of their paycheck but can't buy a $6 latte without a crisis."

Parenting

The slow rescue parent

Lets their kids struggle a bit before jumping in to fix things.

"There's a rare kind of parent who loves their kids deeply, but will absolutely let them struggle with that shoelace for four more minutes."

Fitness

The disciplined snacker

Never misses a 5am workout, never says no to dessert.

"They have the discipline of a Navy SEAL and the self-control of a toddler at a birthday party."

Careers

The one-word genius

The quietly brilliant coworker who answers a long email with "ok".

"There's a rare breed of coworker who can fix the whole project in an afternoon, but replies to your three-paragraph email with 'k'."

Healthcare

The gallows-humor angel

The gentlest bedside manner, the darkest break-room jokes.

"They have the bedside manner of a saint and the sense of humor of a crime scene cleaner."

Business

The chaotic planner

Has a 5-year plan, books the flight the night before.

"There's a rare type of founder who has a color-coded 5-year plan and still books their flight at 11pm the night before."
